item.title: Formal Grammars and Generating Functions: From Algebraic Structure to Non-Algebraic and Non-Derivable Series
item.description: arXiv:2610.33111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates how the algebraic and analytic properties of ordinary length generating functions constrain the grammatical and computational complexity of formal languages. We review the Chomsky-Schutzenberger representation, DSV translations for unambiguous context-free grammars, and their stack-indexed extensions, distinguishing finite algebraic systems from more general constructions. Examples and a diagonal argument demonstrate that even a rational generating function need not determine a language's grammatical class. Our central computability result establishes that, for a recursively enumerable language, computability of its length-counting sequence is equivalent to decidability of membership. Consequently, if a recursively enumerable language has a D-finite length generating function over Q(z), it is decidable; equivalently, undecidable recursively enumerable languages cannot have D-finite length generating functions. We then examine coefficient growth and singularities through Pringsheim's theorem, the Polya-Carlson dichotomy, Hadamard gaps, and Siegel G-functions. The resulting picture is asymmetric: analytic properties provide useful one-way constraints on language computability, but length enumeration loses too much information to determine grammatical or computational complexity without additional assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Zhijun Wang

item.title: Locally eventually onto cellular automata
item.description: arXiv:2610.33131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a new checkable criterion to ensure that a one-dimensional cellular automaton on a finite alphabet is locally eventually onto. In this setting, openness is equivalent to being n-to-1 for some n and therefore implies surjectivity. Bipermutive cellular automata are known to be locally eventually onto, while open cellular automata that are neither bipermutive nor bijective appear to have received less attention. Building on Sutner's work with de Bruijn graphs, we describe a method for deciding openness and at the same time determining n. We then introduce the notion of block-regularity of local rules as a generalization of bipermutivity and prove that it implies openness. We further identify two conditions that, together with block-regularity, ensure that every nonempty cylinder set is mapped onto the whole configuration space after a finite number of iterations, and hence that the cellular automaton is locally eventually onto. The appendix provides the algorithms that check these finite criteria and then presents examples of locally eventually onto, non-bipermutive cellular automata for small diameters.
item.dc:creator: Jan Kristian Haugland, Nadia S. Larsen, Tron Omland, Henrikke G. Rustad

item.title: Verse: Semantics and Verification of Hybrid Multi-Agent Scenarios
item.description: arXiv:2610.35680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifying cyber-physical systems with many interacting agents remains difficult because interactions are mediated by sensors, individual decisions are constrained by environment (map) structure, and the resulting mode space scales combinatorially. We present Verse, a framework for writing agents, maps, and sensors in a familiar programming language syntax, with a formal semantics for the resulting scenarios. A compiler translates each scenario to a hybrid automaton whose executions correspond exactly to the runs of the scenario. Reachability analysis on this automaton builds an execution tree from two post operators, one for continuous flow over a time step and one for a single agent's mode change, and checks safety assertions at every vertex. The tree expands only the modes that are reached, without enumerating the global mode space. Experiments highlight expressive modeling across cars and drones, 2D/3D maps (including OpenDRIVE imports), noisy sensors, and multiple simultaneous safety assertions. Verse verifies a scenario with 7 agents and 37 modes in 90 seconds on a standard laptop; it is competitive with CORA and JuliaReach on ARCH benchmarks, and on multi-agent scenarios is an order of magnitude faster than JuliaReach at the cost of looser reachable sets.
item.dc:creator: Yangge Li, Katherine Braught, Alex Yuan, Sayan Mitra

item.title: Relational Composition as Parallel Transport: What Per-Entity Frames Force in Attention
item.description: arXiv:2610.34945v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A dot product means something only when both vectors share a coordinate system. Content words have one; a fresh entity does not: rotating its coordinates alone changes nothing. We take this per-entity frame freedom as a symmetry and ask what it forces in attention. For orthogonal transports, invariant scores depend only on norms and the transported inner product $\langle x_i,T_{ij}x_j\rangle$; equivariant messages lie in the span of $x_i$ and $T_{ij}x_j$. Endpoint channel count bounds transport rank, so with one vector per entity relations must be supplied; standard attention is the flat sector of a shared frame. Representation theory attaches an integer to each mechanism; the readout decides which. With orthogonal transitions, a convex-cell readout composes a finite group exactly only at or above its smallest faithful real representation dimension. At this minimum, exactness forces a faithful representation. An even readout can decode a cover at smaller width, and the gap is unbounded. Below its threshold, the part of the group a mechanism cannot see sets an accuracy ceiling computable before training. 17/17 fitting seeds at minimal width passed tests through length 1000, versus 7/18 at twice the width; 12 models carry correctness certificates to explicit lengths, from the weights alone. On $C_3\times A_4$ (faithful width 5), descent at width 4 learned the 72-state double cover under sign-blind attention (6/48 seeds; monotone 0/48); on a frozen cover the cross-entropy-optimal affine head is uniform, a quadratic head exact. On parsed CLUTRR, transported composition beats a matched transformer by 41 points at 4-10 hops, but forcing isometries costs 65 points; on StepGame's commutative algebra, isometries help. Static embeddings gave each word one vector; contextual models gave each occurrence its own; per-entity frames make each relation an operator, the unit in which relations compose.
item.dc:creator: Aakash Sarkar, Ananya Mukherjee, Motoshige Sato

item.title: Quantitative Reachability Properties Beyond Decisiveness
item.description: arXiv:2610.35308v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decisiveness is central to reachability algorithms for infinite Markov chains, but is a qualitative notion: it guarantees that path-enumeration algorithms terminate, without an a priori bound on the horizon. We study decisiveness quantitatively of Markov chains, and apply our results to the approximate quantitative coverability problem for effective probabilistic well-structured transition systems (pWSTS). We introduce truncation sets, which represent the horizons sufficient to approximate the reachability probability within a precision $\varepsilon$. These sets reformulate decisiveness quantitatively, and their elements can be computed when it is decisive. To obtain such horizons, before any exploration, we introduce geometrically reachable sets, for which the probability of not reaching them within n steps decreases exponentially in n, up to a prefactor depending on the initial state. Horizons valid for all initial states exist iff this prefactor can be chosen uniformly for boundedly coarse chains. For such pWSTS, including probabilistic vector addition systems and Galton-Watson processes, we obtain a priori global horizons growing at most logarithmically in $1/\varepsilon$. In the non-uniform case, we give a drift condition ensuring the existence of a finite geometrically reachable set. Under this condition, we derive a priori horizons growing at most logarithmically in $1/\varepsilon$ and in the weight w(x) measuring the size of the initial state x. In both cases, we compute a horizon function whose evaluation on any initial state and precision requires only a constant number of elementary operations $(+, -, \times, / \text{ and } \log)$. For probabilistic lossy channel systems, this yields, to our knowledge, the first explicit a priori horizons from arbitrary initial states, and it extends to $\nu$-pLCS, a new infinitely branching variant with probabilistic emissions.
item.dc:creator: Rapha\"el Faure, Alain Finkel, Lina Ye

item.title: SPECOLA: A Tool for Specification Driven Robot Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35730v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulation benchmarks are a useful way to measure progress in robotics; typically they provide success rate as the dominant measure of performance. However, success rate reports only whether a rollout completed the task, hiding by what margin it succeeded, how sensitive the success is to goal parameter changes, requirements it may have violated, and whether success persisted. Signal Temporal Logic (STL) provides a formal language for capturing specifications; it can be used to define requirements, and measure how close a robot behavior is to satisfying or violating them. Using STL monitors in a simulator, however, requires exposing simulator state and mapping it to specification-relevant signals. We present Specola, a tool for evaluating robot behaviors in simulation with respect to STL specifications. Specola provides an interface for writing specifications over simulator signals, and creates and manages the relevant monitors while a policy executes. We provide a Python API and command-line interface for integrating monitoring into existing policy execution loops. We provide an adapter interface for connecting new simulators, and provide adapters for nine simulation environments and benchmarks, including LIBERO, RoboCasa, Isaac Lab, and RoboDojo. We provide case studies that illustrate the nuanced evaluation that Specola enables. Code and adapters are available at https://github.com/specola-eval/specola.
item.dc:creator: Immanuel Ampomah Mensah, Hadas Kress-Gazit

item.title: Certified Split Points for Parallel Lexing: Exact and Modulo Discarded Tokens
item.description: arXiv:2608.03473v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Table-driven DFA lexing is sequential, since each transition depends on the previous byte's state. Scanning one input in parallel needs each chunk's entry state, which existing methods recover by simulation, speculation, prescanning, or overlap. We give two conditions under which none is needed. For a longest-match scanner restarting from q0 at every token boundary, a byte b is a certified split symbol when no reachable state other than q0 has a b-transition whose target can reach acceptance, and q0 is not re-entrant if it has one. Every occurrence of such a byte in completely tokenizable input begins a token, so chunks starting there reproduce the serial sequence of kinds and lengths. The condition is necessary and sufficient, but one string, comment, or whitespace run can remove every useful certificate. Comments and whitespace are usually discarded, so we weaken the guarantee to equality after deleting a declared discarded set and give a second condition, a precomputed constant-time one-bit test. It is sound but incomplete and more permissive, strictly so on suitable token sets and discarded sets. It recovers newline for a conventional C-like tokenization and tab, newline and carriage return for JSON, and refuses newline where block comments are unrestricted. Safety modulo the discarded set is decidable in PSPACE for every token automaton and in polynomial time for literal vocabularies, and every unsafe byte has a replayable counterexample. On the fifteen token sets studied the second condition is already exact. Splitting at exact certificates in munch reaches 92.6-95.3% parallel efficiency at eight threads on a restricted CPU set and a 512 MiB corpus, and a 3.46-3.94x end-to-end speedup at four threads, on one machine. It turns delimiter-based parallel lexing from a language-specific assumption into a property a compiler checks.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: Certified Split Windows for Parallel Lexing: Recovering Boundaries Where No Byte Certifies
item.description: arXiv:2608.09761v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A certified split point lets a parallel lexer cut unlexed input at a single byte with the serial token stream provably preserved, but several conventional token sets in the predecessor's controlled study certify no byte once string, comment, or whitespace-run forms are included (arXiv:2608.03473v2). We generalize from a byte to a bounded window, a byte string after which the position where the current token began is known, regardless of surrounding context. We certify the directly usable form of that recovery, namely that the token covering the window's final byte begins at the reported origin. The certificate is conditional on occurrence and may be vacuous; every applicability figure counts only windows carrying an asserted completely tokenizable occurrence witness. We give a conservative model of a maximal-munch scanner's possible histories across a window, prove it sound, and decide reachability in that model exactly by exhausting a finite quotient of its reachable configurations. Within the flat, completely tokenizable scope, model-positive answers are semantic certificates; negatives are relative to the model, which deliberately refuses some windows a greedy scanner would allow. Whether the model certifies any window, plain or witnessed, is PSPACE-complete, and a shortest window can need $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{n})}$ bytes over n live states. Two smaller searches decide plain model existence, the second shipped in release 2.2.0 of munch. In a sample of 400 random token sets, 322 of the 337 sets certifying no byte gain a witnessed window, with zero inconclusive searches, and every exact-empty row of the predecessor's study gains a witnessed window of two to four bytes. The analysis runs once after automaton construction, using only the compiled tables and no input. A boundary profile marks each gap of a window forced, crossed or open, and a window-local cut is sound exactly at forced gaps.
item.dc:creator: Nicklas Nidh\"ogg

item.title: A characterization of the reversibility of linear cellular automata
item.description: arXiv:2608.20600v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $G$ be a group, let $\mathbb{K}$ be a field, and let $V$ be a $\mathbb{K}$-vector space. We prove that there exists a bijective linear cellular automaton $V^G\to V^G$ whose inverse is not a cellular automaton if and only if $G$ is not locally finite and $\dim_{\mathbb{K}}V \geq |\mathbb{K}|^{\aleph_0}$. In particular, $|\mathbb{K}|^{\aleph_0}$ is the exact dimension threshold for non-reversibility. This answers an open problem proposed by T. Ceccherini-Silberstein and M. Coornaert.
item.dc:creator: Alonso Castillo-Ramirez

item.title: A note on Finiteness and Boundedness in Cartesian Products of Discrete and Well-Ordered Sets, Application to Transition Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.16764v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this short note, we prove that any closed interval in a well-ordered and discrete space is finite. The coincidence between finiteness and boundedness can then be established for transition systems where the state space is well-ordered and discrete. Finally, this result is also proven when the state space is a Cartesian product of $d$ discrete and well-ordered sets.
item.dc:creator: Gerard Memmi
